text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- No more post offices or service kiosks are to be closed down, pledged the head of Posten, Ulf Dahlsten. Rationalisation plans by the post office have caused uproar from customers.
- Sweden has a large shortage of summer jobs, according to Labour Market Board (AMS). AMS said in March there was 2,700 new holiday jobs which was a fall of 1,000 from a year ago.
- Politician Mona Sahlin, who was at the centre of a controversy over misuse of credit cards in 1995, is to return to the political scene in May this year, the paper said.

- Business leader Marcus Storch, chairman of Custos, has dismissed speculation that he will replace Percy Barnevik as chairman of construction group Skanska. Barnevik is to leave to take up the chairmanship at the Wallenberg family's investment vehicle, Investor.

- Analysts applauded the reported plan for Volvo Truck to take over Renault's Mack Truck operations in the U.S.. Analysts told the newspaper that the concentration in this sector in the past 30 years had made it necessary for Volvo to boost its market share to retain a footing. The deal, about which Volvo has made no comment and Renault has denied, would give Volvo Truck a market share of almost 20 percent.

- Clothes sales in Sweden are looking good with higher sales in the past nine months. In March there was an eight percent increase compared with the same period a year ago, according to the latest data from the Retail and Wholesale Research Institute (HIU).

- The national tax authority has appealed to district courts and fiscal courts of appeal nationwide to quickly process all claims involving the alleged asset-stripping activities of financier Bertel Nathhorst. Nathhorst reportedly controls about 1,000 companies which hold 2.3 billion crowns in untaxed profits. Sune Jansson of the National Tax Authority said Nathhorst had made asset stripping his business.

- Sweden's Axel Johnson Saba trading group has announced that it is selling its chain of 360 newspaper shops to Small Shop Holding, a Norwegian firm mainly owned by the U.S. investment bank E.M. Warburg, Pincus & Co.. The Pressbyra shops being sold to Small Shops have combined annual sales of 1.8 billion crowns and a workforce of 2,100. The purchase price was not made public. Small Shops holds the Nordic rights to the 7-Eleven chain.

- The Swedish government will in its spring budget include funding for measures to encourage older workers to retire early, according to newspaper sources. This method of reducing unemployment by shifting older workers out of the workforce is welcomed by public sector employers but private companies are not enthusiastic.

- Stock exchanges in Stockholm and Copenhagen will on April 22 sign a letter of intent regarding increased cooperation, according to some sources. Negotiations between the two bourses have been underway since January.
